Was exploring an alien ruin one time in multiplayer with another dude.

This...[i]thing[/i]...comes charging out of the corner, stabs me, stabs my dive buddy, buddy rag-dolls and gets stuck into its body.

I emptied a magazine into it; it turns around and begins to retreat into the darkness.

I see my buddy get dragged away kicking and screaming deeper into the structure, all the while the thing keeps stabbing him repeatedly.

The screaming on the radio stopped after a while. 

Role-played that I got PTSD from the experience.

9/10

I was a doctor named Dr. Iam Realdoktor (its european) just trying to save my patients (valuable organs). That was until someone attempted to poison me with denatured alcohol. I Injected myself with so many stimulants and detoxers that I was a god. He then tried to fight a god, and was smited by my double barrel which sent them flying across the sub right into the arms of security. I, being a real and good doctor that has a degree in doctoring attempted to save the pathetic life of this mere mortal. I bandaged him up just enough to prevent him from bleeding out. But mistakes happen in the depths, I mixed up my bloodpack with radiotoxin ( a common doctoring mistake), could have been some of the leftover alcohol. His body was melting, even if I would have administered pain killers his body probably wouldnt have helped......probably.  I kept him alive long enough to make sure he felt everything. When he begged me to let him die, I said of course. So I dragged his flesh jello-ed future corpse down into the subs airlock, him screaming with what little air he could muster the entire way. Then ejected him out into the depths and watched as the sheer pressure just created a cloud of red fluid. The notes I have on the event where utterly fascinating.

I am a real doctor. I love the science.

The peak moment of this game was when my friend was frantically running around with the fire extinguisher, yelling over Discord that the submarine was on fire. I headed down to the floor just to see him spraying around, but there was no fire. I hovered my cursor over him and saw the "Hallucinating" effect. 10/10 Realism.

I saw this game mentioned in the comments of a video of Sseth about Space Station 13 and wanted to play it ever since then. A few months ago, an old friend of mine and I decided to play it together while reconnecting after a long time.

I like this game because it greatly rewards good communication, realistic planning and wise decisions. The way you cooperate with others has many layers and you can learn a lot about yourself this way.

It was kinda hard to get a solid group going after my friend went back to his other games. I started visiting random private servers. But it can be hard to find a public server with a good host. So I started my own public server. I put in the effort to be a good but serious captain, to motivate earnest people and quickly sort out problematic randoms and to plan forward and keep morale high.

With a good amount of patience and diligent, perpetuous attention, I built a solid server out of the random players who came at different times during the weekend. We now have a Steam groupchat and a Discord server. We recently finished the campaign, too, which I didn't get to do with the old friend nor in singleplayer.

We bonded over all kinds of terrible situations and epic clutches. Every single one of us grew in the process. We got to know each other in our highs and lows and learned how to talk about everything with mercy as well as severity. And above all, we learned to function as a team in all kinds of situations. This is exactly the experience I was hoping for and I am very glad that I took the leap of hosting my own server.

Barotrauma is obviously a very niche game and it is a niche I uniquely enjoy. I believe that cooperative multiplayer games with great freedom and complexity like this one bring out the whole spectrum of human behaviour. That is too much for most people, but I enjoy it because it means freedom and opens up the possibility for exchanges and experiences which would otherwise not be possible.

It does take effort to take the brunt of all the strange, dishonest, sadistic or also just kinda daft and unworkable people, to fairly talk it out with all of them, give everyone their just "trial" while keeping up the energy (and managing a submarine of eight other people at the same time), but it rewards you with friends who will stick around for some really crazy unexpected rounds of Europan madness. It can feel very punishing but also very rewarding.

I haven't really played with any serious mods yet, but there are good community mods which easily add another hundred hours to the normal campaign, new enemies, weapons, pets, all kinds of items, even musical instruments and much more. The community is wacky, but I kinda like it. The memes are funny.

It's probably not for everyone, but I am very happy with this game.
A simple yet complicated and fun games even without multiplayer, AI is dumb as though so better just do multiplayer for now.
One of the games that make me wait for the action, but when the action comes I beg that it stops

You'll buy this game because it has monsters and submarines, or maybe a streamer you're into played it and it looked like fun. After buying and installing the game, you'll be gently directed to the games very informative and even immersive tutorials. They're well put together and present information in an organic enough way to teach the most adept and promising students how to play the game and be a useful member of a crew. But you aren't here to learn about proper submarine maintenance or social dynamics in confined spaces. You're here for monsters and stuff. You might have a mic, you might not. You might have crippling social anxiety and choose not to use your mic. That's alright, under 10 leauges of icy black death no one's gonna hear your screams anyway, so go ahead and hop right in.

When joining your first lobby, you'll have your choice of job to play. There's captain, but that one seems like it's for people who did the tutorials. Security has a shock baton, that looks pretty cool. Electrician and mechanic look like safe enough bets but you heard from a friend that the deaths of assistants don't count. Perfect.

You're a green horn again. You don't know what to do or where to go. You will have no confidence in your ability to assist but you're pretty sure that this game is gonna be easy enough to learn. There's left and there's right. Control is crouch, e picks stuff up, h will awkwardly pull open the health menu but will also grab onto other players and briefly lock them in place so as to check theirs. This will probably will be your very first interaction with other players in game. You will hear colorful language and instantly create a a lifelong enemy. Don't worry, it's part of the process, trust the process.

Eventually, Captain will call for a dive team and you'll think hey, I'm not doing anything. You'll grab a suit and 3 extra tanks because you're a good little Johnny and you are really gunning for that A+. Two other divers are waiting in the airlock for you. They say hurry, you hurry. When you're all in, a button is pushed and the three of you are jettisoned out into the abyss. There is a serene moment of calm floating, suspended in the dark with your dive team. The moment is brief however, as your team mates pull out strange scooter devices that you might have seen on a nature documentary once and scoot off screen. You are now alone.

If you're now panicking, it's probably a good thing. Your oxygen is now finite and your ability to fix this situation is depleting as quickly as your 3 bottles of survival. This will be your introduction to the chat functionality. R will swap between radio and local chat. V will activate your mic but you don't have a mic you have social anxiety remember? Pressing T will open the text chat. Alright, you can do this.

You tell the crew that you're alone and scared. Someone tells you to swim up, you swim up. Like a small child lost in a Super Walmart, you're very trusting right now. You wonder if the relief that you feel as you see the light on the airlock is generational, but you don't have time to think about that right now. Someone is explaining what the scooter is, where it can be found and how to maintain the battery on it, but you don't have time to think about that right now. Someone has said the word 'Breached' over the radio and something about the urgency in his voice tells you that you very much have to time to think about this, right now. 

You ask the person closest to you what you can do. He gives you a wrench and a screwdriver, tells you to equip them, and shows you how to use them and quickly runs out of the room saying that he'd be back. As you begin repairing panels and getting better at the repair minigame, the game becomes kind of calming again. You almost feel talented as the panels get repaired and stay repaired. As your skill improves bit by bit, it's almost easy to ignore the strange, violent sounds you hear in the rooms near you. Almost.

Combat is easy enough to understand. Hold right click to prepare a strike and left click to unleash it. You could probably use your wrench and screwdriver to do some amount of damage, but you already learned what happens when you go around touching crew mates. You decide it's best to avoid any friendly fire incidents, besides, combat is probably best to avoid this early in your assisting career. So you continue running around the sub repairing junctions boxes and the occasional motor. When you run out of junction boxes, you'll find a welding tool and start repairing the hull. Switching to this job without instruction will make you feel smart. See? You don't need no "tutorial", with that fancy "book learning". You got that good old fashioned American can-do. We've won wars like this.

In the coming years when you think about this day, you'll remember how quickly the veil of your reality splintered. Fractured into nothingness. To pin point the exact moment your innocence was lost seems equal parts possible and pointless. It might have been the slowly building silence in which your confidence grew, like a crab in boiling water. It might have been the bodies. Was it the realization that no one was screaming, or that no one had checked on you? This must be what hell feels like.

When the hull is repaired, and the junction boxes aren't smoking anymore you'll have a second to think. Pressing G will cause you to begin dragging unresponsive allies. As you gather the dead, you press H just to see what it looks like, but it feels disrespectful so you stop. You wonder what happened but you will never find out. As the only survivor of this tragedy, you know that it's your imagination. But you swear you can hear a voice. A quiet voice from no where, whispering in your ear, "The deaths of assistants don't count."

Then maybe their lives do. Maybe the assistant is more than the tutorial class. Like a pawn in chess, the assistant's value isn't known until the end, bitter as it may be. You'll remember every trial and tribulation you've faced, every bully you've conquered. With one last push of confidence you approach the navigation terminal. How hard can it be?

Pretty hard. You switch the sub to manual and go up, this has worked for you in the past. After a few moments of going up you find the cave ceiling. You crank the sub back down rapidly. You can tell by the flickering of light and crackling of electricity that the sub did not like that. But wait, you're still moving down. You smash the sub into the sea floor and decide that assistance is not needed on helm. You have several new breaches to deal with. 

You're losing hope. Your crew is dead and hasn't ended the game yet. They're all watching you. In your frustration, you begin hitting the walls with a crowbar you found but there's no point. Water is creeping up the bottom layers of the sub. You think about the old Nietzsche quote about the abyss. It is up to your knees. As you stand in the face of death, powerless to stop it, you think back on what you could have done differently. The water is to your waist now. To your shoulders. As it enters your nose and mouth you'll think, this is my home. I'm coming home.
Tbh i've played the game illegaly for more than 1000hr+ and just now able to paid the game after my first job, VERY RECOMENDED!

So I'm new to the game, finally get on a sub with a group of randoms keen to work together and not grief. Its a large sub I've never been on, so I don't know my way around.

But it's going well, I'm wrenching things up like a good mechanic creating solutions for problems... Until the power goes out. Unfortunately the engineer and half the crew are outside the sub on a diving expedition. Fuck it, it's just powering the reactor I can handle this, right?

So I start poking the reactor with my screwdriver... Power seems low. Pull the levers it's not getting better. Ok, I'll stick another rod in there?

KABOOM. FIRE. FUCK ME

Why doesn't this reactor room have a fire extinguisher?

Half dead from the explosion I race upstairs to find one, grabbing a diving suit on the way (why I dunno) and finally found an extinguisher near the engine room.

Then I race back and the entire reactor room is ablaze. No worries, I got my extinguisher. So I open the door while wildy, pathetically spraying extinguisher everywhere but the flames are too intense and I die almost instantly.

The captain comes racing down to save the medic in the room next door but it's too late the medic's already dead and the flames are still getting bigger. Meanwhile, the others get back from their diving mission. One of them sees the dire straights in our section, heads on down and says "I'm doing this for the greater good" .... Then he detaches the whole section we're in, leaving the captain stranded with us sinking away from the sub!

How!?

If I have this right, this reactor was in a spawning vessel (?) attached to the main sub. So we're sinking and the captain is frantically running around and somehow miraculously manages to put the fire out, repair the vessel, then steer it back and re-dock with the sub.

An absolutely phenomenal experience, and one of the best co-op games I have played, ever.

This game is in a tough spot to review, as at least in my opinion it requires at least 2 people to be enjoyed fully, or at all to be honest. It's not the usual case of "more fun with friends", I'd say it's more along the lines of "barely any fun at all alone". Does this make the game bad? For some yes, most definitely so. But this game, when played with friends, reaches heights of enjoyment I have not experienced in a long time, and definitely not with a price tag as affordable as Barotrauma.

The atmosphere in this game is without comparison. The lighting, the ambiance and the sounds all compliment each other perfectly. It has a coherent style that fits the eeriness and dread that are oh so apparent during your underwater journey. I recommend using the in-game voice chat when playing with friends, as it adds a whole another layer of immersion and gameplay. You cannot speak to others if you lose consciousness, get paralyzed or die etc. and the haphazard rescue missions and possibly even the tragic recovery of a body after you realize that someone is not answering, is one of the strongest examples of top tier psychological horror and co-operation present in any game to date. It isn't supposed to be how much you can communicate, or how loud, or even how often. It is what you communicate and how, what is important. In this game I understood how truly powerful silence could be. It's very hard to put into words how Barotrauma handles this aspect of co-op, as it is something far more instinctive and fluid compared to the usual. You are not there to boost your friends over a fence, you are there to catch them when they fall. 

The game mechanics are quite simple, but flexible enough to create many situations that are hard to foresee and prevent. Even the most simple of choices can backfire on you when all chaos breaks loose. Have you ever tried to find a tiny wrench in a pitch black maze of steel that keeps filling with water at an ever-increasing rate? After playing Barotrauma, I have. Needless to say, that character of mine did not make it, along with many others. Yet, not a single time did I think my life, or my friends for that matter, was on the hands of some evil entity cheating and ruining our experience. It was always our own fault, and noticeably so. This flawless continuation of new events leading to discovery and improvement is so often lackluster in todays games, even though it is immensely rewarding and enjoyable. Barotrauma manages to capture the essence of this cycle. How often have you lost all tangible currency and every single item in a game and had to start over, and yet still thought to yourself "Man, I feel so much stronger now." 

Calling Barotrauma a game would be a disservice to it. I am not being grandiloquent for no reason, I am perfectly serious. Barotrauma is an experience. It is a rare piece of media capable of actually elevating gameplay to a level of seriousness that you actually become invested in the game. There were times that the characters on screen were actually the people I knew in real life. I was actually scared of losing them, I was actually terrified of being the last one alive. Instead of yelling something stupid and throwing myself to the mercy of the deep sea, I was careful and proactive. And most importantly, I felt there was something on the line. The moment I started to doubt my own capability, my ability to actually progress in the game, I knew that this was no ordinary game.

The singleplayer aspect of this game lacks all of the above. You are truly alone and on the mercy of bots that don't always even know how to traverse the ship, wasting time and resources. It is hectic and difficult to control the ship alone while commanding the bots to do tasks. There is no communication and no co-operation. The game feels dull and empty. When your ship gets attacked instead of scared you feel annoyed. There is no one to ask, no one to guide and no one to rely on. If you plan on playing this game alone, just know that it isn't even tenth of the experience you get with the help of a friend, even a single one. And if you play with friends, just disable the bots, they are not great. 

The bots are the worst part of the game, but not entirely awful by any means. I hope they see some improvements in the future. Apart from that this game doesn't need much else, just more content. And maybe the terrain could be a bit prettier, but that's just my opinion. 

Singleplayer 5/10
Multiplayer 10/10

[After 450+ hours of gameplay and some updates I thought I should add some notes]

Alright, here are the facts.

If you want to play this game on single player, as of right now, forget about it. This game's single player is unpolished with an extremely limited AI. Every Barotrauma player will agree that everything great about this game is in multiplayer. [AI is getting better but still needs work]

Yes, there are griefers in the game, but they represent a minority. People overexagerate with this in the reviews. It's not that bad. On the vast majority of occasions, your crew will be over 90% loyal and the griefer will be found and executed promptly. After a while, you will quickly identify them just by watching them interact with the ship and crew. Personally, although I don't enjoy griefers in this game, I think they add a nice touch since they are pretty much the crazy guy in horror movies who ends up on a killing spree. It adds a chaotic variable to the game and hunting him down with the crew is fun and fixing whatever was broken adds a nice challenge to the game.

Talking about challenge. I've seen people complaining that this game is hard. It's not. It's the way that you and your crew play it that makes it easy or hard. If you have newbies and idiots on board, you will have a harder time. If you have experienced players instead, it'll be so easy that you will readily go against the hardest objectives the game has to offer and will even want to raise the overall difficulty of the game ( because yes, there is a difficulty bar for those who are having a hard time ). In a sense, the difficulty of this game reflects the difficulties you could have in real life. Not everyone is an equal in real life in any domain whether it be in a business or in a sub.

Don't see defeat as defeat. See it as an experience. This game is not about winning or losing, it's about doing your best to overcome the obstacles. It's about the journey between the start and finish line.

This game is something else when it comes down to multiplayer interactions. That's what I love the most about it. I once read another player who perfectly captured the essense of it all by saying: you have to trust your teammates, but never entirely because you never know what might happen. Mistakes will be made, treachery and mutiny can occur. In a sense, this is the most human oriented simulation ever made in video game history. Somehow, I can imagine sailors have met extremely similar situations throughout history.

The game is in development but it set everything up to build on a solid basis. The physics, visuals, sound effects and atmosphere is all there. All they need to do is to fix some bugs and add some more content. They should focus on simplifying character, creature and item creation. Sub creation is great as it is. This game is still in early access as we speak. Don't let those who claim it's dead deceive you. It's just underwater, but it will come to the surface soon enough. You need to be patient with these guys. They're not a billion dollar company and don't have unlimited staff. Anybody who has played this game just a little bit knows it has potential. And I know this potential will be achieved. [The game has constant updates, most recently they added tons of stuff for the campaign which is now much more popular online]

Finally, I'd like to say that if you really want to enjoy this game, you have to let go of reality. You have to stop being a player and be a captain, an engineer, a medic, a mechanic, an assistant or a security officer. You have to immerse yourself in the game to truly grasp its magic. You have to talk as if you're in a real sub and your in-game life has to have the value of your real life and the same goes for the life of your crewmates. Only then will you truly understand how great Barotrauma is. [I still agree!]

( One more edit: I'd like to point out that over time, I somehow ended up being a moderator on Barotrauma's Steam forum. This in no way means that my review was/is biased in any way. I'm just a total nutcase who fell in love with this game. )

While walking through a city that my AI crew and I had only just arrived to, I get a prompt stating that "You hear a noise coming from inside the vent in the room". This being the first port on our journey and my first time playing since the update, I hadn't considered that anything dangerous would happen. Especially inside of a crowded, occupied space. I shined my light inside to see what was causing the noise and THREE mud-raptors EXPLODE out of the vent! I, the Captain, was launched out of the door of the room and across an open two story space to the bottom floor. While severely injured from the fall and somehow being bitten multiple times, I managed to instruct my three, hapless crew members to Rescue & Aid before losing consciousness. By some miracle, while running through a crowded room full of gunshots, teeth, and screaming people, one crewman managed to find my body and begin CPR. To my surprise, I was successfully revived and immediately attempted to fire on the creatures without injuring fellow terrified victims of brutal mutilation. In the end, despite surviving the ambush and the amazing heroism of my crew, I succumbed to severe internal injuries ten minutes later. 

  The latest update is what this game has needed for a long time. The improved AI now performs far better than I ever thought it would. I'm honestly impressed with all the improvements that have been made and I am excited to continue seeing support for this unique game.

I strongly recommend this game, conditionally.  

The game is quite brilliant.  The graphics look very simple, but once you start playing that quickly stops being important. The game is wacky, and scary, and it can be a heck of a lot of fun. You can easily get into the atmosphere of surviving in the harsh unforgiving waters of Europa. There is a lot to do here. There are many adventures to be found. There are many perils to face. You will make mistakes. You will die. But with experience you might also learn how to survive and even thrive.

It is important to understand that Barotrauma is not a solo experience. None of the subs are designed with solo play in mind. You are expected to have a crew to do things. You are expected to have a crew to operate the sub. You are expected to have a crew to handle the perils you will face when you go on a dive. This is not a game you are expected to play alone. 

The sub editor can help with this if you are willing to spend the enormous amount of time and brainpower necessary to master it. The sub editor is quite powerful. You have free reign to design a sub however you like. You can make subs that are friendlier for small crews or even solo play if you insist on that insanity. 

But, Europa is still a harsh and unforgiving world. And it just isn't very much fun to try to play this game solo. You want friends. So I need to talk a little bit about the community here.

The community loves chaos. The community is not your friend.

Trying to play this game with randos from the barotrauma community is a recipe for disaster. Many of the people who might join your game are only interested in causing problems. They might shoot you. They might stab you. They might inject you with weird drugs. They might set of explosives in your submarine. In short, they will just try to grief you in any and every way that they can.

Many of them will be obvious about it. Many of them will hurry to cause trouble as quickly as they possibly can. Others might show a tiny bit more restraint and wait for you to let your guard down a little before trying things. Others might be alright, at least until they get tired or bored. 

There are game modes that encourage this sort of behavior. They are irrelevant. Griefers are never going to care about that. Griefers need to grief.

So to wrap things up, yes, I do recommend this game, conditionally. I have played it lot. I have used the sub editor extensively. And I have had glorious adventures with my friends. You just need to make sure you bring real friends for this adventure. If you try to sail with randos your voyage is not likely to end well.

A very fun game session where we were trying to take down a Swarm, that went something like this:

1. Our Sub was attacked not only by the Swarm, but also by a BONE TIGER TRESHER (Actually by 2 of them)

 2. So then, our Sub goes down and runs out of power. Our Coilgun stops working, and we still have like 3-4 fish eating out our hull.

3. The Security guard gets the brilliant idea to go out of the airlock, which would've been fine if he didn't only have a stun baton on him. And we also only find out about his brilliant idea as he tries to swim back to the airlock while being chased by the Thresher. He didn't make it.

4. So here's the situation. There are three people left. Me (the Captain) Our Doctor, and our Engineer. The Sub is basically wrecked, it's entirely submerged in water and everything that is electronic and else is completely fecked.

5. Our Engineer, basically our main way to survival, walks out into the flooded command room without a diving suit and gets crushed by water pressure. His last words? "What the fuck."

6. Our remaining crew, ie: Me, Doc, (and our helpful ghost of the Engineer) come up with an ingenious plan. Go outside and shoot all the feckers. Of course, our Security guard may have failed before us, but unlike him we actually had guns. Things go wrong right off the bat, however. As I exit out of the airlock with my SMG, ready to turn that dumb Thresher into Swiss cheese, our Doctor gets stuck trying to open the airlock door while uttering the words: "Oh my god, this game's controls suck so badd!".

7. So i'm outside alone. Me, vs the Tresher. All I have on me is an SMG with 2 mags. I look up and notice the Tresher gunning it straight to me, and as I empty the entire mag into him - we collide. I get hit with internal damage and I start bleeding. My Doctor? Still stuck at the airlock. Great. The big Tresher, albeit damaged already before our encounter, is now at half-health. My health is also draining exponentially, and blood loss is accumulating fast. I quickly drop my empty mag and reload my SMG, as the Tresher is preparing to collide into me again, I drop my second mag into him. He gets stunned for a few seconds, 1/4th of his health remaining, I quickly switch to my revolver and finally put him down. Mission accomplished, whew.

8. My Doctor finally makes it out of the airlock (very conveniently). I'm bleeding profusely, and i'm near death. Panicking, I get back into the Sub while frantically screaming "I'm bleeding help help help i'm gonna die!!". The Doctor tries to chase me down as i'm running all around the place trying to find medical items, forgetting that our Doc is actually the man with all the supplies. Long story of running around short, I finally calm down and he miraculously saves me from near death. Sweet.

9. However, our mission is not fully accomplished yet. The Sub? Still Submerged. The Tiger Treshers? There's still one left. Hotel? Trivago. We go out on one more outside venture (This time making sure the Doc actually goes with me). We make it to the second Thresher and unload all our ammo into him. The fecker still lunges at me even though the Doctor is much closer. We put him down, at the cost of me starting to bleed again. However, the threat was finally over, albeit we had much more work ahead of us.

10. So all the fish were finally dead, including the Swarm. Now, our next task was to bring our ship back from complete submergion. An arduous and a not really worthwile task, however we were not about to step down from a challenge.

11. We welded. We fixed. We struggled. After a loong while of fixing all the leaks and junction boxes, we finally were able to bring the Nuclear Reactor back online, and pump out all the water. Hurray. Or did we?... As the power turns on, and "all" the water pumps out, we finally breathe a sigh of relief. This is probably a good time to point out that throughout all this time, we were stuck about 190 meters away from the station. We could smell victory. It was so close, yet so far. I make it back to the piloting station. "Finally!" I think to myself, "We're gonna actually win!" However, tragedy struck again. Our Sub? It refused to move, and remained completely stationary. Confusion and panick all go through my body at the same time. 

12. I find out the reason of our unableness to move. Our Oxygen refilling room? It was completely flooded. We go and investigate, however our search determines very little. There are no obvious leaking walls around the area, yet the room keeps being filled with water. Clearing the room proves to be futile. Our first ingenious plan was to break through the bottom floor of the room to check for outside leaks. However, tragedy strikes for perhaps the last time. Our beloved Medic, who went through this entire grandeur journey with me, replaced his diving suit Oxygen tank with a Welding Fuel tank. His last moments were filled with him sniffing petrol, perhaps a nicer death than our other crewmates, but still.

13. At this point, I was the last man standing, But for my comrades, I had to keep going, for otherwise their sacrifices were futile. I put our plans into motion, and break through the Oxygen room's floor. Aaand there was nothing under. Still no leaks were visible. I was confused, sad and angry at the same time. My options were running thin. Our helpful Engineer ghost (Who died way earlier in the run) had a suggestion: "Maybe try to check out the pump in the room? See if you can pump all the water out?". I check the pump... And that's when it all clicks together. The pump? It was pumping the water into the room. This entire time it just kept flooding the room. Over, and over. Our Doctor died for nothing. The Discord channel erupts in laughter.

14. However, I was not going to let it all be for nothing. I was determined to finally finish this fecking mission, no matter the cost. I definitively get rid of the water on the sub, and got back to the helm... Movement! I can finally leave.

One does not simply summarise or declare things about Barotrauma. This game is, at its surface, simple. You get in a sub, and go from point A to point B - transporting, salvaging, or killing your way between them. But after some time you begin to realise that this isn't just a survival game - it's a game about true, slow-building terror. The darkness is oppressive, and horrors very much do reside within it. You will perish if you are caught off guard. You will perish if your inventory restock two stations back was not as comprehensive as it should have been. You will perish if you don't flick that sonar off at just right moment - and even if you do everything right, sometimes something you couldn't have seen coming rises from the darkest depths and takes you anyway. 

But Barotrauma isn't just about that - it's also about rising to the occasion, it's about standing as a beacon of resilience in the dark of what could be all that remains of humanity, it could be the end, this mission could be the last lifeline a station has, the last chance to survive another month, or save the sickly - this game isn't just about YOUR survival, it is also about being strong enough that others make it out too. And if you do your goddamned best to be that beacon in the dark you see the results of your courage and perseverance, a return of mild prosperity on this frozen fucking rock. 

Barotrauma is a game about oppressive darkness, horrors very much within our comprehension and desperation - but Barotrauma is also very much a game about courage, heroism and mag-dumping through the fear. 
Don't pass this game up, trust me.

[h1]Quite long Review, but if you are on the fence, give this a read [/h1]

Barotrauma is a great game with a well thought out design for groups of players especially. You feel like a real explorer with a crew to back you up and just like the character traits in the game, everyone has their own personal ticks that make the game more fun and enjoyable. When your crew is at maximum and plans all thought through it is fun to see how far you have come as you fly through areas.


[b]Positives: [/b]
[u]1) Group Game[/u]
Every Class fills an important role on the ship, except Assistant... ew. Every class can encapsulate a different gamer's personality.

[u]2) Mechanics[/u]
Simple mechanics like falling and breaking your legs on a huge ship are really funny even though it should be annoying. 

[u]3) Horror[/u]
The game gets more fun the worst things get, your medical officer has been gardening for the past couple of rounds?
BOOM THE MEDICAL QUARTERS ARE ON FIRE AFTER HOURS OF GROWING EXPLOSIVE PLUMS! 

You find an underwater palace that looks like it was made by the gods?
"HOLY **** THERE ARE THINGS KILLING US IN HERE! SWIM! SWIM! SWIM AWAY!". 

"I'm sure this 6 skull quest will be fine, we have taken on 1 of these things before, I'm sure it will be fine"
CRASH! *All onboard lights turn red*
"EVERYONE BATTLE STATIONS! GET YOUR WEAPONS READY, THEY ARE BOARDING! SOME OF YOU MAY DIE BUT THAT'S A SACRIFICE I AM WILLING TO MAKE!"
*As your captain runs to grab a diving suit instead of preventing the ship from plummeting*

[u]4) Mods[/u]
Mods for this game are pretty damn cool, increasing the size of ships you explore is my favourite as it also adds more enemies to random encounters, turrets, and with more to explore, comes more treasure. Higher risk, higher rewards. 

[u]5) Creation[/u]
The ability to make really cool stuff and have improvements past the first iteration is awesome. I think we have almost unlocked the best oxygen tanks in the game and it's amazing to see our level meaning something. Rather than in games like Skyrim (example) where you only get something every 20 and it takes forever and by the time you reach the end of the game you really don't need half of the random stuff you have to unlocked.

[u]6) Updates[/u]
The developers have put real effort in, had a vision for an interface, and a team game that works well.


[b]Negatives: [/b]
[u]1) Death Patch[/u]
After a recent patch, death doesn't just take away some health for a long period of time but resets your character's skills. You could be a level 200 in steering and it could have taken 10/15 hours of in-game time to reach that and suddenly a breach in the hull sweeps you off your feet, you die instantly from the pressure and suddenly you're back to square one at level 50 at best. This was a horrible decision from the developers, please change this to losing 20 or 30 points in your top skills or something similar. We end up resetting more often than not as we really just want to have fun and not spend another 3/4 hours making wrenches just to get that Mechanical Engineering skill up. 

[u]2) Ew[/u]
Assistants... Ew, just ew. Are these creatures even allowed on ships?

[u]3) AI or just A in this case[/u]
I tried to do the single-player campaign but honestly, I would rather drive screws in between my toe nails, the AI don't listen to anything outside of fix or follow which means you have to kill everything, pilot everywhere, build everything, and control the reactor all by yourself. 
There is an order to turn on the reactor, I spent 20 minutes telling the crew to do it through commands and ended up doing it myself. Instead of continuing, realising every time we would run out of fuel I would have to do it myself. I shot the whole crew, then committed suicide before quitting to play exclusively with real people and never return. AI are good at following simple commands 

[u]4) Glitches[/u]
Glitches are unavoidable, especially with this physics engine, but basically the biggest glitch is when a creature (usually small) gets stuck in the hull somehow and we have to usually injure ourselves to kill it. 


[b]Improvements:[/b]
[u]1) Deaths[/u]
As mentioned a better system should be implemented for death, it's not fun and honestly makes people on my ship want to quite with how much it pulls away from the experience. It's fun to make cigars and random bio husk mods, but when you die and then go to make them and joke around about it, you immediately remember, oh yeah I can't do that until I play another 5 hours. If you could control this or change the setting so people could still choose to have it, that would be good I think. 

[u]2) Host Improvements[/u]
I like that you can set different abilities for different players like banning, kicking, buying , and so forth. However, I have to set this with every new lobby I make, could you set it so depending on lobby name or create a file that stores these options for each player on the hosts computer or something like that. 

[u]3) Difficulty control [/u]
As I mentioned in the death one, my friends and I are quite far into the game and we even have to change our ship because of crushing depth now which is an awesome feature that we never thought about until we got warnings about it. However, I feel like enemies are a little too easy, granted we still die, but I would love to change the difficulty at will, even if it's just in the lobby as we really don't want to start over, but I feel like we could be beaten up more. 

[u]4) Random encounters[/u]
More random encounters with clowns and messed up things please, I would love for things to be a little more random in the depths. Getting attacked by a random pirate/bandit ship would be cool. 


[b]Conclusion: [/b]
If you are looking to get stuck into a group game, where communication is key, everyone feels useful, and the world can be as you make it, this is the game for you, the world is interesting with a lot to explore. 

I would recommend at least 3 people, as you need a captain, engineer/mechanics, and another who can help fix and fight or just fight, medic/security. 

Keep in mind that like a job in real life, not every role is going to be as fun for you as it could be for another, it is personality thing. 

[b]Roles:[/b]
1) If you like talking and telling people what to do, the captain is for you. 
2) Like messing around, shooting things and being the man with the gun, security will be good for players who just want to hang out with friends as it's a simpler role. 
3) Medic is similar to security but you must be willing to put you gun up last as everyone will be relying on you out in the field to learn how to heal people as quickly as possible. Being someone who likes to learn crafting, mastering a game mechanic, and messing about with everyone's genetics without consent will be good for you.
4) Mechanic and engineer is for those who like to master a craft as well, although one will be more focused on the ship's inner workings and one the hull/equipment. 
5) Assistants are for slimy sewer rats with no hope at a real world relationship with a human... Ew.

The single player has much to be desired and will make you want to kill everyone, although if you can play it, it apparently has a lot more interesting NPC interactions within the world.

If you actually read all this, I hope to get to the bottom of the planet and continue playing with my crew for a long time.

This game isn't finished, and in many ways, it shows - the mechanics can be difficult to understand at first, and it takes quite a bit of time to really master the systems, but once you do, oh man is it a satisfying game.

I've only played the singleplayer campaign so far, and am getting ready to build my first submarine. Holy shit is that like a world unto itself. But all the rest is good too, and the game openly and extensively supports modding to boot, with a substantial refactor due soon to make it even easier. It's a great time to start checking this out, but I'd say it's also an equally good idea to wait until full release. There's a lot of stuff that still needs work, but the foundation is incredibly solid, and the devs are definitely working hard on it. Major updates come out multiple times per year.


The complexity involved in building and customizing submarines is absolutely insane, in a good way. It's simple to get going, but can range all the way to the extremely complex. You don't just plop down an engine, reactor, nav terminal, pumps, and a few guns, then call it a day - OH no. You gotta wire that shit together [i]manually[/i], with actual wires you place and run through the ship, with all sorts of logic components you can intersperse between devices to create complex systems. People are creating their own PID controllers to manage the reactor for fuck's sake (or just doing the extremely simple but effective bang-bang controller method)! And you can do most of this stuff IN-GAME, not just in the editor! Absolutely amazing capabilities here. I can see this devouring hundreds more hours of my life as I try to tweak and optimize complex automation. So stoked.

And, fortunately, the actual wires never go bad or get damaged, only the endpoint devices. So that at least makes your life slightly easier when everything is going to hell.


As for the gameplay itself, I love it, mostly. Exploring the depths of Europa, getting attacked and fixing the sub during a shitstorm, going EVA once things quiet down to mine materials and explore or salvage wrecks, then heading on to the next outpost for new missions... it's a good gameplay loop. 

The things I dislike about it have less to do with the core gameplay design and more do to with balance or jank that could be smoothed over with some QoL passes. These are things that can more or less be addressed with further development or, at worst, mods (so, not so bad!).


As of the Rising Tide update, these are the biggest things I think still need work:


* Game performance. The game is horrendously unoptimized, and can become unplayably choppy on even decent hardware with 16+GB of RAM, especially on larger subs or with more than 4 or 5 bots in your crew. This is all vanilla stuff, too.

You'll also notice huge lag spikes when big colonies of enemies spawn in, which is not only bad for the performance, but immediately clues you in to their proximity and, thus, that you should prepare for attack. Big shitstorms where enemies breach the sub and flood everything are already chaotic enough to deal with (which is good) on their own, but adding extreme lag to that makes it reeeeeeeally frustrating sometimes. I've restarted missions because of lag making it basically impossible for me to respond effectively to anything with 5-10 second input delays.


* Campaign difficulty balance / difficulty controls: the game is EXTREMELY easy in some respects, particularly making money and finding resources.

In the very earliest stages of the game, you'll feel tight on cash and supplies, but after you've gotten half way through the first biome, you'll start wondering why the sub has so little storage space. If you are low on supplies of ANY kind, just take on a wreck salvage mission, or go exploring on your own and you'll almost certainly find one, and they almost always have TONS of loot you can deconstruct or sell.

It's way, way too easy to amass a stockpile of supplies so large you'll start running out of room to place things well before you run out of critical survival equipment or reactor fuel. This can be countered somewhat by turning on Jovian Radiation, but I don't think this would outright solve the issue, and it's kind of a lame way to handle it (it basically just makes it almost impossible to backtrack, urging you in one direction, whereas by default it's a lot more freeform and gentle with the progression).


* Inventory management can be a pain in the ass, especially on small subs, and especially due to the aforementioned overabundance of resources. In the early game, if you're at all curious and like exploring, you WILL run into this. You'll end up making storage containers to fill every inventory slot since those can each hold 12 items of their own, so instead of 8 chunks of iron (max for one stack), you can now fit 96 chunks into the same space... but you have to do a lot more clicking to manage everything. Why not just allow 96 chunks in the first place, then, and make it so the player's personal inventory can only take up to 8 at a time? Spare me from having to have a dedicated storage container for every random resource, please! There are A LOT of those, and all of them come in great quantities before long.

Yes, the game takes a more classical approach to inventory stacking, which is good and bad: you won't have to worry about oxygen tanks using up all your storage capacity due to their volume, but you can't store two screwdrivers in the same slot, either. Some sorta bizarre choices here, but most of it you just kinda get used to and work around. Doesn't mean it's not a flaw, though!

Also, some of the vanilla subs are HORRIBLE with storage capacity despite their spacious interiors, which I don't understand -- is it a balance thing, or for performance reasons? Some subs also have their own fabrication and deconstruction suites, but NO STORAGE IN THE SAME AREA (or not nearly enough), so you'd have to run back and forth carting shit around just to do basic construction operations (looking at you, Remora. That's the main reason I picked the Winterhalter when I needed a deep diver!).


* Bot AI is mostly pretty good, but occasionally they still do braindead things, like kill themselves in the ballast tank while trying to grab a loose item that has gotten fused into a wall (which was ripped open during an attack, then repaired later, but the item remained in the gap). They can't reach the item, but they will try their damndest, even ignoring basic needs like oxygen, and won't ever give up. You have to tell everyone to hold the fuck up so they won't go immediately fix the hole you have to go cut yourself to retrieve the empty oxygen or welding fuel tank, etc, then restore their orders.


* The campaign is still very unfinished, especially the story and ending, but I expect this is actively in development so it's not a huge deal right now. I hope the faction system gets fleshed out a lot more, as right now there's not really any importance to it. It's also trivial to end up Revered by literally everyone if you just do missions (which you'll need to do to make money early on anyway). [h1] Sailing the waters of Europa is a harsh and unforgiving experience. [/h1]

Barotrauma is a cooperative horror game in which you and your crew must work together to ensure the submarine sees success on its missions. Everyone has their role on the sub, and each is just as important as the last. This game can be played solo with bots, or multiplayer up to 16 players. The settings in-game are customizable enough, setting more XP gain, world hostility, etc to better suit the way you want to play.

[h1] Your Crew [/h1]
There’s 6 roles in the game to keep people busy.

First off is the Captain who pilots the submarine, gives orders, all that. Most of his time is spent staring at a sonar, but he’s the one who in most cases will be making the decisions for the entire crew. The gameplay loop is avoiding ice spires and terrain, and keeping good angles for the people manning the guns.

Second is Engineer. He’s going to be maintaining junction boxes and working the reactor. It’s in all honesty a bit of a boring job but it has to be done. His upgrades allow him to eventually craft nuclear weapons, so it’s not all bad. With a smaller crew, Engineer seems fine as a bot.

Next up is Security, these are the guys who will be maintaining order in the submarine following strict order from the Captain. They’re the ones manning the guns and keeping YOU from being fish-food. One of the more fun roles in the game, in my opinion.

Fourth is Mechanic. They fix pumps, fix hull breaches, and just all around repairs. They’re kind of just waiting for things to happen so they can be a bit boring from time to time, but they are invaluable. For reasons below I prefer my mechanics to be players, but most of the time the bots are fine. Like the Engineer, it's not all bad. Mechanics have the skill to create full mech suits, which are ridiculously powerful and benefit everyone. They aren't even that hard to craft, either.

Then we have the Doctor. He’s either going to save your life or inject you with husk eggs. Let’s hope it’s not the latter. They’ll heal you better than you can do for yourself, so if you’re able to, let the doc treat you up rather than rushing and wasting supplies needlessly. For the same reason as the mechanic, they can be a bit boring to play sometimes.

Lastly, we have the Assistant. The assistant does not specialize in anything in particular, so not really much to be said. More of a “jack of all trades, master of none” type thing going on.

In the worst case scenario, any role will be able to do someone else’s job. Selecting your role is more so just selecting specialties, in which you would be able to do a specific role better than others.

[h1] Bots are okay for the most part. [/h1]
Playing with bots is somewhat frustrating at times, but they are very good at their jobs otherwise. I've had half my crew die because they prioritize their diving masks rather than diving suits, and by the time they realize they need a diving suit instead, they crush due to pressure. Many missions reloaded because I'm not spending 10k marks to replace them for such a stupid mistake. You also have to watch them when they load your guns, I've had several times in which they just randomly have a nuke loaded into my railgun and me blasting off rounds at something up close just for that nuke to be jumbled in next in line spontaneously aaand... entire submarine is bricked and the whole crew is dead.

Other than those complaints, the bots are actually pretty great. Zero issues with a bot engineer manning the reactor for the most part, security on turrets get the job done, doctors will usually be pretty quick to rescue. Mechanics on the other hand are hit or miss. Sometimes they're slow at repairs due to the fact they'll get in there to fix the hull breach just to go back to try and grab a diving suit realizing they're in danger. They'll eventually get the job done assuming they don't die to water pressure. Having bots follow you outside the sub, they don't seem very good. I've had them get briefly stuck in areas such as submarine doors or turns inside of a cave. Most of the missions are completely fine going out there solo anyways as long as the submarine is parked close by, so it's a non-issue for me.

[h1] Players will always be better than bots. [/h1]
I think it goes without saying, but a human will always be better. They aren't letting themselves die to obvious dangers, and are going to be a lot more fun than managing bots. Whether it be goofing off or roleplaying, a human player will have your back better than a bot ever could. While this game is definitely playable and enjoyable with bots, the experience is only enhanced with a crew of players. There's a lot of downtime in which you're managing your supplies on the submarine. Bots can't really help you with that other than putting some boxes on some shelves.

[h1] Horrors of Europa [/h1]
Unfortunately, the water isn't all you have to worry about. There are life forms outside of your submarine, and they want you. The targets can range from small annoyances to horrible abyss monsters. Having security on guns with eyes open is the only way you can reliably fight back. You will learn to despise Hammerheads and Tiger Threshers as they will tear your submarine up and have you falling deep below where no man willingly enters. Mag-dumping these bastards has never felt more necessary than now.

[h1] Safe Zones and Factions [/h1]
In Barotrauma, you are moving from station to station, completing missions for factions, restocking on supplies whenever needed. There's 4 factions, although admittedly the factions don't really add too much to the game. Rising your reputation with one faction might lower another. Higher reputation will open pathways for your submarine, give better deals with merchants, etc. Lower reputation will keep pathways closed, give you ball-bustingly high prices, and even get to the point where you are denied entry from stations (but docking your sub there is still fine) and shoot on sight will be enforced. It's there, but that's all I can say about it as no story or real gameplay change is featured within them. It’s probably also important to mention that it’s really just 2 “major” factions plus 2 smaller, minor factions. They’re all small, but the majority of your missions are going to be for the Coalition or the Separatists.

[h1] The missions [/h1]
Throughout the game, you’re going to be able to choose the missions you want to do via selecting your pathway. Some of the missions can feel repetitive, but only if you don’t mix it up very often and only choose ones you’re comfortable with. Obviously, some missions are harder than others, but will award more marks for you to spend. There’s also about 5 different biomes you’re passing through, so visually it won’t be too long before you see something new.

[h1] It's a great game. [/h1]
There is a lot of depth to it (no pun intended) with crafting and resource management, and it's honestly a lot simpler than it first seems after you spend a couple hours trying things. If you like games like Project Zomboid, you'll probably love this game.

[h1] The only flaw… [/h1]
It’s the price tag. It is so hard to convince anyone to try this game when it's $35. It’s so much fun but it’s still $35 and if you can’t convince your buds to get it, you're stuck with either bots or random players you don't know... which as always is VERY hit or miss. If you can get over that hurdle that is the price tag, this game will suck you in faster than opening a flooded room. Good luck in your adventures!

The game can be a mixed experience. Some players might find it boring due to the long campaign, griefing teammates, or having to play solo because of a lack of friends. For me, most of the fun came from building submarines with advanced systems using dozens of logic gates, heavily decorating them to tell a story through the designs and rooms, or modifying built-in subs. I’d guess at least 70% of my playtime was spent in the sub editor, I'm not joking.

Overall, you like building subs? Or managing crews? Go for it. Otherwise you might have a bit of a bad time.

I’m generally not a huge fan of anything related to aliens or the ocean, but Barotrauma is one of those games you simply can’t pass up. There’s something about it that grabs you right from the start, even before you fully understand what that something is. This isn’t the kind of game you dive into for a quick evening of play and forget about. It demands time, attention, and patience, but in return, it offers an experience unlike any other.

Basically, Barotrauma is a survival simulator set on a submarine, stranded deep in the hostile waters of Europa — one of Jupiter’s moons, where death can strike from anywhere: reactor malfunctions, oxygen leaks, grenade-wielding clowns, or an open hatch at the wrong moment. Every mission is a struggle for survival, set against the backdrop of technical failures and internal chaos. It’s less about action and more about managing constant disorder, where teamwork is your only chance to stay afloat. Sometimes it feels less like commanding a submarine and more like desperately trying to keep it from falling apart. And that's where its charm lies. You don’t return to Barotrauma because it’s easy, but because it’s endlessly interesting. Every session is a new story, a new disaster, a new “almost made it, but…”

Visually, the game is more intriguing than frightening. It doesn’t push you away; rather, it charms you with its muted color palette and clean, minimalist art style. The simple yet expressive 2D graphics work perfectly with the sound design. There is music in Barotrauma, with each outpost having its own unique track depending on its specialization. This creates an atmosphere that makes you want to linger there just a little longer before embarking on your next dive. Outside these areas, there’s the game’s tense atmosphere maintained through sounds — muffled thuds, creaking hulls, footsteps — each contributing to a feeling of unease without ever drawing too much attention to itself.

This is one of the few games where, even after hundreds of hours, you can still stumble upon something new — a mechanic, an event, or a bug you didn’t know about before. And that’s a rare and valuable thing. This unpredictability keeps every run feeling fresh and prevents the game from becoming stale.

Each role is an invitation to experience something different. Not only does each new profession provide a reason to learn new mechanics, but I often found myself choosing the more attractive initial branches in the skill tree at the expense of overall efficiency. The game leaves room for improvisation, and no one is afraid of making mistakes — those are just part of the learning process. Sometimes you’ll be patched up by others, sometimes you’ll figure things out on your own, but it always gets more exciting as you progress. 

The game doesn’t forgive mistakes, but surprisingly, there’s always a place for newcomers — as long as you’re willing to listen and learn the mechanics.  If you don’t know where to start, just ask someone, and they’ll guide you. Starting as a mechanic, engineer, or assistant is usually the best way to learn without disrupting the team's efforts. One of the best features is that, before starting a campaign, the settings go well beyond the standard "Easy-Abyssal" difficulty scale. Every parameter can be adjusted individually, allowing you to truly customise the gameplay experience to your style.

The AI won’t fully replace a real player, but it performs admirably in most of its duties — especially considering the developers are continually improving it. Solo campaigns aren’t as vibrant as multiplayer, but they provide a safe space to learn the ropes and experiment. It’s convenient to switch between roles and gradually familiarize yourself with each of them. On moderate difficulty, bots are generally adequate, but they do have their limits, especially in more complex scenarios.

However, it’s the multiplayer that really makes Barotrauma shine. This is where the game truly comes into its own. Every role — from engineer to medic — is vital, and teamwork isn’t something forced upon you, it’s simply necessary for survival. Each session with a new team feels like a fresh playthrough. Sometimes you’ll be with veterans, other times with beginners, and each time, the experience will unfold differently.

The replayability of Barotrauma is exceptional. Even after dozens of runs, you’ll want to come back — try a new role, a different submarine, or a different way of interacting with the world. It’s not about grinding and forgetting; it’s about continuous evolution. Some professions are better suited for solo play, while others truly shine in a well-coordinated team. But regardless of what you choose, there’s always room for growth and discovery. As you grow, the game becomes more enjoyable.

The emotions of victory and defeat are especially vivid in this game. The joy of surviving against the odds, the fear of decompression, the nervous laughter during an accident — these moments stick with you. You never quite know how things will end, and yet, you return. PvP in Barotrauma isn’t the main draw, and personally, I didn’t find it especially exciting, but as a break from the main campaign, it’s perfectly fine.

The Barotrauma community is generally more calm than in other co-op or competitive games. Sure, there are a few trolls, but they don’t stick around for long. Finding a server with the right playstyle and pace can be tricky, but when you find the right one, it feels like a perfect fit. It’s convenient that you can read the server description beforehand to see if it suits your playstyle — this makes finding a comfortable spot much easier.

And of course, for those who decide not to stick with the vanilla game, the modding community is always active. The workshop is full of addons and mods that can radically alter gameplay, add new mechanics, maps, characters, and much more. This allows you to tailor the game to your liking, beyond the original design. Modders have significantly expanded and diversified the game, adding everything from new gameplay features to creative content that can refresh the entire experience.

Barotrauma is a game open to creativity, and this is reflected in its wide variety of components, including the ability to create custom submarines, characters, or even monsters directly within the game. This level of customization encourages players to create something unique and share it with others. The modding options broaden the horizons, letting players put their own spin on the game.

Every hour spent in this game has been worth the money, and while there’s still room for improvement, it undoubtedly deserves a positive review.
